goals: Describe how cells were discovered and state the cell theory
Compare plant and animal cells, and prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, with examples
Explain the function of the nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, vacuoles, plastids and cell wall
Use magnification to find the actual size of a cell from a drawing

slides.heading: Cell: the unit of life
slides.body_md: Part 1: how cells were found, what kinds there are, and what the parts inside them do.

visual.alt: Table of the approximate sizes of four cells, from tiny to very large

slides.narration: Every living thing you can name, from a banyan tree to the bacteria on your skin, is built of cells. Most are far too small to see without a microscope. A few, like the yolk of an ostrich egg, are huge. In this part we learn how cells were discovered, how plant and animal cells differ, and what the tiny parts inside a cell do.

slides.heading: How cells were discovered
slides.body_md: A **cell** is the basic structural and functional unit of life. Cells were found only after microscopes were invented.

rows: Saw box-like compartments in a thin slice of cork and called them cells
Saw living single cells, such as bacteria and pond organisms, with a single-lens microscope
Concluded that all plants are made of cells
Concluded that all animals are made of cells
Stated that new cells arise only from existing cells

visual.alt: Table of five scientists, the year and what each found about cells

slides.narration: In sixteen sixty-five Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork and saw many small box-like rooms. He called them cells. Later Leeuwenhoek used a single-lens microscope and saw living cells in pond water. In the eighteen thirties Schleiden and Schwann said that plants and animals are made of cells, and Virchow added that new cells come only from old cells.

slides.heading: The cell theory
slides.body_md:
Three ideas together form the **cell theory**:

1. All living organisms are made of one or more cells.
2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function.
3. All cells arise from pre-existing cells.

nodes.label: Hooke sees cell walls in cork
Schleiden and Schwann: plants and animals are made of cells

visual.alt: Flow of four steps in the development of the cell theory

slides.narration: The cell theory grew step by step. First came the sight of cells, then of living cells. Then Schleiden and Schwann joined plants and animals under one idea. Virchow completed it. Today we say three things: all organisms are made of cells, the cell is the unit of structure and function, and every cell comes from a cell that already existed.

slides.heading: Cells differ in size and shape
slides.body_md: Cells are measured in **micrometres**. One millimetre is one thousand micrometres. Shape follows job: a nerve cell is long and thin, a red blood cell is a small flexible disc, a plant cell in a stem is long and tube-like.

visual.alt: Table of four cells, their shapes and how each shape suits the job

slides.narration: Cells come in many shapes and sizes, measured in micrometres. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre. A nerve cell is long and branched so that it can carry signals far. A red blood cell is a small disc that squeezes through narrow vessels. A root hair cell has a long thin extension that reaches more of the water in the soil.

slides.heading: Worked example: size from a drawing
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A student draws an onion peel cell. The drawing is 24 mm long and the magnification is 400 times. Find the actual length of the cell in micrometres.

**Step 1.** Magnification $= \dfrac{\text{size of drawing}}{\text{actual size}}$, so actual size $= \dfrac{\text{size of drawing}}{\text{magnification}}$.

**Step 2.** Actual size $= \dfrac{24\ \text{mm}}{400} = 0.06\ \text{mm}$.

**Step 3.** Convert: $0.06\ \text{mm} \times 1000 = 60\ \mu\text{m}$.

visual.alt: Flow showing the steps from drawing size to actual size in micrometres

slides.narration: Here is how to find the real size of a cell. Divide the size of the drawing by the magnification. That gives the actual size in millimetres. To change millimetres into micrometres, multiply by one thousand. For the onion cell drawn twenty-four millimetres long at a magnification of four hundred, the actual length is sixty micrometres.

slides.narration: Look at the plant cell. Outside the thin cell membrane is a rigid cell wall of cellulose, which gives the cell its fixed shape. A large central vacuole filled with cell sap pushes the nucleus to the side. Green chloroplasts capture light for photosynthesis, and mitochondria release energy. The endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus handle proteins and other products.

slides.heading: An animal cell
slides.body_md: An animal cell has **no cell wall** and no chloroplasts. Its nucleus is usually near the centre, and its vacuoles are small.

slides.narration: Now the animal cell. It has only a flexible cell membrane, so animal cells can change shape and can have many forms. The nucleus often sits near the centre. Vacuoles are small, and there are lysosomes, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum and a Golgi apparatus. There are no chloroplasts, so an animal cell cannot make food by photosynthesis.

slides.heading: Plant cells and animal cells compared
slides.body_md: Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, ER and Golgi apparatus. They differ in the features below.

visual.alt: Table comparing plant and animal cells on six features

slides.narration: Plant and animal cells share many parts, such as the membrane, nucleus, mitochondria and Golgi apparatus. The differences matter in exams. Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, one large central vacuole and chloroplasts. Animal cells have no wall and no chloroplasts, and their vacuoles are small. Plants store food as starch, while animals store it as glycogen.

slides.heading: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
slides.body_md: In a **prokaryotic** cell the DNA lies free in a region called the **nucleoid**, with no nuclear membrane. A **eukaryotic** cell has a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

visual.caption: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells: schematic, not to scale.

slides.narration: Cells fall into two big groups. In a prokaryotic cell, such as a bacterium, the DNA lies in a region called the nucleoid. There is no nuclear membrane and there are no organelles with membranes. In a eukaryotic cell, the DNA is inside a true nucleus, and organelles such as mitochondria and the Golgi apparatus are wrapped in membranes.

slides.heading: Quick check: kinds of cells
slides.body_md: Decide whether a cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask yourself one question first: is the DNA enclosed in a nuclear membrane or not?

slides.heading: Examples and differences
slides.body_md: Prokaryotes are mostly unicellular and small. Eukaryotes include single-celled organisms such as *Amoeba* and yeast, as well as all plants, animals and fungi.

rows: No nuclear membrane; DNA lies in the nucleoid
True nucleus with a nuclear membrane

visual.alt: Table comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells with examples

slides.narration: Here are the differences in one place. Prokaryotes have no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Their DNA is usually one circular piece, and the cells are small. Eukaryotes have a true nucleus, organelles with membranes, several chromosomes and larger cells. Bacteria and cyanobacteria are prokaryotes. Amoeba, yeast, plants and animals are eukaryotes.

slides.heading: Nucleus, ER and Golgi apparatus
slides.body_md: The **nucleus** holds the DNA and controls the cell. The **rough ER**, studded with ribosomes, makes proteins; the **smooth ER** makes lipids and helps remove harmful substances. The **Golgi apparatus** modifies, packs and dispatches products in small sacs called vesicles.

nodes.label: Ribosomes on rough ER make protein
Vesicle carries it out of the cell

visual.alt: Flow showing the route of a protein from the nucleus to the outside of the cell

slides.narration: Think of a cell as a small factory. The nucleus holds the instructions, written in DNA. Ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum build proteins by following them. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum makes fats and helps to remove harmful substances. The Golgi apparatus then modifies and packs the products into vesicles, which carry them to where they are needed.

slides.heading: Mitochondria, lysosomes and vacuoles
slides.body_md: **Mitochondria** release energy from food in respiration, so they are called the powerhouses of the cell. **Lysosomes** hold enzymes that digest worn-out parts and germs. **Vacuoles** store water, food and wastes.

rows: Stores water, food, wastes; keeps plant cells firm

visual.alt: Table of mitochondria, lysosomes and vacuoles with their structure and job

slides.narration: Mitochondria have two membranes, and the inner one is folded. They release energy from food during respiration, which is why we call them the powerhouses of the cell. Lysosomes are small sacs of digestive enzymes that break down worn-out parts and germs. Vacuoles are fluid-filled sacs for storage. In plants, the large vacuole also keeps the cell firm.

slides.heading: Plastids and the cell wall
slides.body_md: **Plastids** are found only in plant cells. **Chloroplasts** contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis. **Chromoplasts** hold coloured pigments, and **leucoplasts** store starch, oil or protein. The **cell wall** is made of cellulose and is fully permeable.

rows: Outside the membrane of plant cells

visual.alt: Table of three kinds of plastid and the cell wall with their places and jobs

slides.narration: Plastids are found only in plant cells. Chloroplasts are green because of chlorophyll, and they carry out photosynthesis. Chromoplasts give petals and ripe fruits their colours. Leucoplasts are colourless and store starch, oil or protein, for example in a potato. Outside all this, the cellulose cell wall gives shape and protection. Water and dissolved substances pass through it freely.

slides.heading: Worked example: which cell is it?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A student sees cell P under the microscope. It has a thick boundary outside the membrane, a large central sac and green oval bodies. Cell Q has a thin boundary only, many tiny sacs and no green bodies. Name the kind of cell in each case and give two reasons.

**Step 1.** Thick outer boundary, large vacuole and green bodies: cell wall, central vacuole and chloroplasts.

**Step 2.** So P is a **plant cell**. Q has no wall, no chloroplasts and small vacuoles: an **animal cell**.

visual.alt: Table linking observed clues to plant or animal cell

slides.narration: Work like a detective. Cell P has a thick boundary outside the membrane, a large central vacuole and green oval bodies. These are a cell wall, a vacuole and chloroplasts, so P is a plant cell. Cell Q has only a thin boundary, many small vacuoles and no green bodies. It has no wall and no chloroplasts, so Q is an animal cell.

slides.body_md: Match an organelle to its job.
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the job of each organelle, and decide which one fits the clue in the question.

Prokaryotes have no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have both.
Nucleus controls; mitochondria release energy; ER and Golgi make and pack products; lysosomes digest.
Actual size equals drawing size divided by magnification.

Prokaryotes have no true nucleus. The nucleus controls the cell, mitochondria release energy, the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus make and pack products, and lysosomes digest. slides.heading: How cells exchange and divide
slides.body_md: Part 2: water and dissolved substances crossing the membrane, and how one cell becomes two.

rows: Salt draws water out of a pickle

visual.alt: Table linking four everyday events to the cell idea behind each

slides.narration: Why do dried raisins swell in water? Why does salt draw water out of raw mango pickle? Why does a wilted bunch of palak freshen up in a bowl of water? The answers lie in how substances cross the cell membrane. This part also shows how one cell divides into two, so that you grow and wounds heal.

slides.heading: The membrane is selective
slides.body_md: The **plasma membrane** is **selectively permeable**: it lets some substances pass freely, others slowly and some not at all.

visual.alt: Table of four kinds of substance and how easily each crosses the cell membrane

slides.narration: The plasma membrane works like a careful gatekeeper. Small molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide pass freely. Water passes through easily. Glucose and ions pass slowly, with the help of special carriers. Large molecules such as proteins and starch cannot pass. We call this property selective permeability.

slides.heading: Diffusion
slides.body_md: **Diffusion** is the movement of particles from a region of **higher concentration** to a region of **lower concentration**, caused by their random motion. It needs no energy from the cell.

rows: Near the stick to the whole room
Ink in a glass of water

visual.alt: Table of four examples of diffusion in daily life and in cells

slides.narration: Diffusion is the spreading of particles from where they are crowded to where they are fewer. You notice it when the smell of incense reaches the next room, or when a drop of ink colours a whole glass of water. Cells use diffusion to take in oxygen and let out carbon dioxide. Diffusion needs no energy from the cell.

slides.heading: Osmosis
slides.body_md: **Osmosis** is the net movement of **water** through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration, that is, towards the stronger solution.

slides.narration: Osmosis is diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane. Look at the funnel. The sugar solution inside has less free water than the pure water outside. So water moves in through the membrane. Sugar molecules are too big to move out. The level in the stem rises. Water always moves towards the region with more dissolved substance.

slides.heading: Activity: an egg in water
slides.body_md: Soak a raw egg in vinegar for a day to dissolve the shell. The thin **membrane** remains. Weigh the egg, then place it in pure water. In another set-up, use a strong sugar solution.

visual.alt: Table of the result of placing a shell-less egg in pure water and in strong sugar solution

slides.narration: Here is a simple activity. Soak a raw egg in vinegar for a day. The shell dissolves, but a thin membrane remains. Put the egg in pure water, and it swells as water enters by osmosis. Put another in a strong sugar solution, and it shrinks as water leaves. Weighing the egg before and after shows the change.

slides.heading: Activity: raisins and the potato osmometer
slides.body_md: **Raisins:** dry raisins swell in water and stay shrunken in strong sugar solution. **Potato osmometer:** scoop a cavity in a potato, add sugar, and stand it in water. Water enters and the sugar solution in the cavity rises.

visual.alt: Flow of the four steps in the potato osmometer activity

slides.narration: Two more activities. Drop dry raisins into water, and they swell as water enters. Keep others in strong sugar solution, and they stay shrunken. For the potato osmometer, scoop out a cavity, put sugar in it and stand the potato in water. Over a few hours, water enters through the potato cells and the level of liquid in the cavity rises.

slides.heading: Worked example: potato strips
slides.body_md:
**Problem (data given).** Four potato strips of $10.0\ \text{g}$ each are left for an hour in sugar solutions of different strengths. The table shows the final mass. Find the strength at which the mass would not change.

**Step 1.** Percentage change $= \dfrac{\text{final} - \text{initial}}{\text{initial}} \times 100$. For 5 percent sugar: $\dfrac{10.3 - 10.0}{10.0} \times 100 = +3$ percent. For 10 percent: $-6$ percent.

**Step 2.** The change goes from $+3$ to $-6$ between 5 and 10 percent, a swing of 9 over 5 units.

**Step 3.** Zero change is $\dfrac{3}{9}$ of the way: $5 + \dfrac{3}{9} \times 5 \approx 6.7$ percent. At about this strength the solution is isotonic with the potato cells.

visual.alt: Table of the masses of four potato strips before and after one hour in sugar solutions (given data)

slides.narration: Let us use data. Four potato strips of the same mass were kept in sugar solutions of different strengths. Work out the percentage change in mass for each. In pure water the strip gains, and in strong solutions it loses. The change goes from a gain to a loss between five and ten percent sugar, so the no-change point lies between them, at about six point seven percent.

slides.heading: Quick check: osmosis
slides.body_md: Predict the direction of water movement.
slides.narration: Quick check. Compare the two sides of the membrane, and decide which side has more dissolved substance.

slides.heading: Hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions
slides.body_md: In a **hypotonic** (weaker) solution water enters the cell: **endosmosis**. In an **isotonic** solution there is no net movement. In a **hypertonic** (stronger) solution water leaves: **exosmosis**. A plant cell that loses water shrinks away from its wall: **plasmolysis**.

slides.narration: Compare the solution outside with the cell sap inside. In a weaker, or hypotonic, solution water enters the cell. This is endosmosis, and a plant cell becomes firm and turgid. In an isotonic solution there is no net movement. In a stronger, or hypertonic, solution water leaves the cell. This is exosmosis, and a plant cell shrinks away from its wall. That is called plasmolysis.

slides.heading: Osmosis in daily life
slides.body_md: Osmosis explains many everyday events. Roots take up water by osmosis, and the turgid cells keep leaves and stems firm.

slides.narration: Osmosis is at work around you. A wilted bunch of palak becomes crisp in water because its cells take water in. Salt sprinkled on cut raw mango draws the liquid out. Roots absorb water from soil by osmosis. Drinking sea water does not quench thirst, because the strong salt solution draws water out of your body cells.

slides.heading: Cell division: mitosis
slides.body_md: **Mitosis** makes two identical cells from one. It gives growth, repair and replacement of worn-out cells. The chromosomes are copied first. The stages are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.

nodes.label: Metaphase: line up in the middle

visual.alt: Flow of the stages of mitosis from prophase to two daughter cells

slides.narration: Before a cell divides, its DNA is copied. In mitosis, the chromosomes become visible in prophase, line up in the middle in metaphase, and the copies are pulled apart in anaphase. In telophase two new nuclei form, and then the cytoplasm divides. The two daughter cells are identical to the parent. Mitosis gives growth, repair and replacement of cells.

slides.heading: Cell division: meiosis
slides.body_md: **Meiosis** occurs in reproductive organs to make **gametes**. One cell divides twice to give four cells, each with **half** the chromosome number. Fertilisation then restores the full number.

slides.narration: Meiosis is the division that makes gametes, which are sperms and egg cells, or pollen and egg cells in plants. A cell divides twice and gives four cells, each with half the number of chromosomes. When a sperm fuses with an egg at fertilisation, the full number is restored. Mitosis keeps the number the same, and meiosis halves it.

slides.heading: Worked example: counting chromosomes
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An onion root-tip cell has 16 chromosomes. (a) How many chromosomes in each cell after three rounds of mitosis, and how many cells? (b) How many chromosomes in an onion gamete?

**Step 1.** Mitosis keeps the number: each cell still has 16. Three rounds give $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ cells.

**Step 2.** Meiosis halves the number: $16 \div 2 = 8$ in each gamete.

visual.alt: Table of cells and chromosome numbers after mitosis, meiosis and fertilisation in onion

slides.narration: Let us count. An onion root-tip cell has sixteen chromosomes. After one round of mitosis there are two cells, after two rounds four, and after three rounds eight cells, each still with sixteen chromosomes. Meiosis halves the number, so each onion gamete has eight. When two gametes fuse, the zygote has sixteen again.

sections.heading: 1. Discovery of the cell and the cell theory
sections.body_md:
Cells were seen only after microscopes were made. **Robert Hooke** (1665) looked at thin cork and named the box-like compartments *cells*. **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek** (1670s) saw living single cells in pond water. **Schleiden** (1838, plants) and **Schwann** (1839, animals) said that organisms are made of cells, and **Virchow** (1855) said that new cells come only from existing cells.

The **cell theory**: (1) all organisms are made of one or more cells; (2) the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; (3) all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

Cells are measured in micrometres: $1\ \text{mm} = 1000\ \mu\text{m}$. **Magnification** $= \dfrac{\text{size of drawing}}{\text{actual size}}$.

sections.heading: 2. Plant cells and animal cells
sections.body_md:
Both kinds have a **cell membrane**, **cytoplasm**, a **nucleus**, mitochondria, ER and Golgi apparatus. A plant cell also has a cellulose **cell wall**, a large central **vacuole** and **plastids**. An animal cell has none of these three, and its vacuoles are small.

Plants store food as starch and animals as glycogen. The cell wall gives the plant cell a fixed shape and lets it become firm (turgid) when it takes in water.

sections.heading: 3. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
sections.body_md:
In a **prokaryotic cell** the DNA lies in the **nucleoid**, not enclosed by a nuclear membrane, and there are no membrane-bound organelles. Bacteria and cyanobacteria are prokaryotes. They are usually about 1 to 5 micrometres long.

A **eukaryotic cell** has a true nucleus with a nuclear membrane and organelles with membranes. *Amoeba*, yeast, plants, animals and fungi are eukaryotes, and their cells are usually 10 to 100 micrometres across.

An organism whose cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
The region of a prokaryotic cell where the DNA lies.

sections.heading: 4. Cell organelles and their functions
sections.body_md:
- **Nucleus:** double membrane with pores; holds DNA in chromosomes; controls the cell; has a nucleolus.
- **Mitochondria:** double membrane, inner folds; release energy from food in respiration (powerhouses).
- **Endoplasmic reticulum:** network of membranes. *Rough* ER has ribosomes and makes proteins; *smooth* ER makes lipids and helps remove harmful substances.
- **Golgi apparatus:** stacked sacs that modify, pack and dispatch products in vesicles.
- **Lysosomes:** sacs of digestive enzymes; break down worn-out parts and germs.
- **Vacuoles:** store water, food and wastes; the large plant vacuole keeps the cell firm.
- **Plastids:** chloroplasts (green, photosynthesis), chromoplasts (colours), leucoplasts (store starch, oil, protein).
- **Cell wall:** cellulose, in plants; shape and protection, fully permeable.

key_terms.definition_md: The organelle that holds the DNA and controls the activities of the cell.
The organelle that releases energy from food during respiration.
A small sac of digestive enzymes.
A green plastid containing chlorophyll, where photosynthesis takes place.

sections.heading: 5. Permeability, diffusion and osmosis
sections.body_md:
The plasma membrane is **selectively permeable**. **Diffusion** is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration. **Osmosis** is the net movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane towards the region of more dissolved substance.

Activities: a shell-less egg swells in pure water and shrinks in strong sugar solution; dry raisins swell in water; in a potato osmometer the level rises as water enters the sugar solution in the cavity.

In a **hypotonic** solution a cell gains water (**endosmosis**) and a plant cell becomes turgid. In a **hypertonic** solution it loses water (**exosmosis**), and a plant cell shows **plasmolysis**. In an **isotonic** solution there is no net movement.

sections.heading: 6. Cell division and recent advances
sections.body_md:
**Mitosis** gives two identical cells with the same chromosome number: growth, repair and replacement. Stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then the cytoplasm divides. **Meiosis** happens in reproductive organs: two divisions give four **gametes** with half the chromosome number; fertilisation restores it. A cell with $2n$ chromosomes gives gametes with $n = 2n \div 2$.

Recent advances (textbook level): **stem cells** can divide and become specialised cells, and bone marrow transplants are an established use, while many other uses are still being researched. **Fluorescence microscopes** light up chosen parts of a cell with dyes. **Electron microscopes** show structures too small for light microscopes. **Cell culture** grows cells in a dish for testing medicines.

key_terms.definition_md: Division that gives two identical cells with the same chromosome number.
Division in reproductive organs that gives four cells with half the chromosome number.
A sex cell, such as a sperm or an egg, with half the chromosome number.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that bacteria have "no nucleus" instead of "no true nucleus; DNA lies in the nucleoid".
- Saying that solute moves in osmosis; it is water that moves.
- Mixing endosmosis (water enters) with exosmosis (water leaves).
- Forgetting that meiosis gives four cells and halves the chromosome number.
- Labels in diagrams that do not touch the part they name.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a definition, a name or one function.
- 2-mark items: two differences or two reasons, one mark each.
- 3-mark items: a short description with an example.
- 5-mark items: a labelled diagram (about 2 marks) and a clear explanation.

cards.front_md: Who first saw and named cells, and in which material?
cards.back_md: Robert Hooke, in 1665, in thin slices of cork.

cards.front_md: What did Leeuwenhoek see that Hooke could not?
cards.back_md: Living single cells, such as bacteria and pond organisms.

cards.front_md: State the three ideas of the cell theory.
cards.back_md: All organisms are made of cells; the cell is the unit of structure and function; all cells come from pre-existing cells.

cards.front_md: Who added that new cells arise from existing cells?
cards.back_md: Rudolf Virchow, in 1855.

cards.front_md: How many micrometres in one millimetre?
Formula to find actual size from a drawing?
cards.back_md: $\text{actual size} = \text{size of drawing} \div \text{magnification}$

cards.front_md: Three features found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
cards.back_md: Cell wall, large central vacuole and plastids (chloroplasts).

cards.front_md: What is the plant cell wall made of?
cards.back_md: Cellulose.

cards.front_md: How is food stored in plant cells and in animal cells?
cards.back_md: Starch in plant cells; glycogen in animal cells.

cards.front_md: What is a prokaryotic cell?
cards.back_md: A cell with no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; its DNA lies in the nucleoid.

cards.front_md: Give two examples each of prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
cards.back_md: Prokaryotes: bacteria, cyanobacteria. Eukaryotes: Amoeba, yeast, plants, animals.

cards.front_md: Usual size of a bacterium compared with an animal cell?
cards.back_md: Bacterium about 1 to 5 micrometres; animal cell about 10 to 100.

cards.front_md: What does the nucleus do?
cards.back_md: Holds the DNA and controls the activities of the cell.

cards.front_md: Why are mitochondria called powerhouses of the cell?
cards.back_md: They release energy from food during respiration.

cards.front_md: Rough ER versus smooth ER?
cards.back_md: Rough ER has ribosomes and makes proteins; smooth ER makes lipids and helps remove harmful substances.

cards.front_md: What does the Golgi apparatus do?
cards.back_md: Modifies, packs and dispatches products in vesicles.

cards.front_md: What is held inside a lysosome?
cards.back_md: Digestive enzymes, which break down worn-out parts and germs.

cards.front_md: Why does a plant cell have a large vacuole?
cards.back_md: It stores water and cell sap and keeps the cell firm.

cards.front_md: Name the three kinds of plastid and their jobs.
cards.back_md: Chloroplast (photosynthesis), chromoplast (colour), leucoplast (stores starch, oil or protein).

cards.front_md: What does selectively permeable mean?
cards.back_md: It lets some substances pass and not others.

cards.front_md: Define diffusion.
cards.back_md: Net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration.

cards.front_md: Define osmosis.
cards.back_md: Net movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane towards the stronger solution.

cards.front_md: What happens to a shell-less egg in pure water, and why?
cards.back_md: It swells, because water enters by osmosis.

cards.front_md: Endosmosis versus exosmosis?
cards.back_md: Endosmosis: water enters the cell. Exosmosis: water leaves the cell.

cards.front_md: What is plasmolysis?
cards.back_md: Shrinking of the protoplast away from the cell wall when a plant cell loses water in a hypertonic solution.

cards.front_md: Which solution makes a plant cell turgid?
cards.back_md: A hypotonic (weaker) solution.

cards.front_md: What does mitosis produce, and what is it for?
cards.back_md: Two identical cells; growth, repair and replacement.

cards.front_md: What does meiosis produce, and what is it for?
cards.back_md: Four cells with half the chromosomes; gametes.

cards.front_md: An organism has 24 chromosomes in a body cell. How many in a gamete?
cards.back_md: 12 (halved by meiosis).

cards.front_md: Name two recent advances in cell biology.
cards.back_md: Stem cell research and electron or fluorescence microscopy.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: what do you write for osmosis?
cards.back_md: Water moves through a selectively permeable membrane towards the stronger solution.

questions.stem_md: A single-lens microscope was used in the 1670s to report living single cells in pond water for the first time. Who made this report?

options.text_md: Robert Hooke
Matthias Schleiden
Rudolf Virchow
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek

questions.solution_md: Hooke saw only the walls of dead cork cells. Leeuwenhoek was the first to see living single cells, such as bacteria and pond organisms, so the answer is option (d).

questions.stem_md: A village teacher claims that bacteria appear by themselves in boiled, sealed dal water, with no bacteria present at the start. Which idea of the cell theory does this claim go against?

options.text_md: All cells arise from pre-existing cells.
All organisms are made of cells.
Cells can be seen only with a microscope.
The cell is a unit of structure and function.

questions.solution_md: If bacteria appeared with no earlier bacteria, new cells would form from non-living matter. That contradicts the idea that cells come only from existing cells, option (a), stated by Virchow.

questions.stem_md: In a school laboratory a student draws a leaf cell 45 mm long. The microscope magnification is 500 times. The actual length of the cell is:

options.text_md: 90 µm
9 µm
900 µm

questions.solution_md: Actual size $= \dfrac{\text{size of drawing}}{\text{magnification}} = \dfrac{45\ \text{mm}}{500} = 0.09\ \text{mm} = 90\ \mu\text{m}$ — option (a). (b) and (c) slip by a factor of ten in the conversion; (d) multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of features is found in a plant cell but NOT in an animal cell?

options.text_md: Nucleus and mitochondria
Cell membrane and cytoplasm
Ribosomes and Golgi apparatus
Cellulose cell wall and a large central vacuole

questions.solution_md: Both kinds of cell have a nucleus, mitochondria, membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and a Golgi apparatus. Only plant cells have a cellulose wall and a large central vacuole — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A plant cell has a fixed shape, but an animal cell can change its shape.

**Reason (R):** A plant cell is surrounded by a rigid cell wall made of cellulose.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: The rigid wall holds the plant cell in shape, while the animal cell has only a flexible membrane. R is the correct reason for A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The box-like cells that Hooke saw in a thin slice of cork were living cells.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Cork is dead tissue, so Hooke saw only the empty walls of dead cells. Living cells were first seen later by Leeuwenhoek.

questions.stem_md: Hooke named the compartments he saw in cork “cells”, from a Latin word meaning a small ______.
questions.solution_md: The word “cell” comes from the Latin cellula, a small room.

questions.stem_md: Hooke looked at thin cork and Leeuwenhoek looked at a drop of pond water. State one difference between what the two scientists saw.

answer.model_answer_md: Hooke saw only the empty walls of dead cells, which looked like tiny rooms. Leeuwenhoek saw living single cells that moved and fed, such as bacteria and other tiny pond organisms. His single-lens microscope gave clearer images of living things.

questions.solution_md: Dead cell walls against living cells.

marking_scheme.step: Hooke: dead cell walls in cork
Leeuwenhoek: living single cells in pond water

questions.stem_md: A leaf cell and a cheek cell are placed side by side. Give two features, other than the nucleus, that you would use to tell the two apart.

answer.model_answer_md: The leaf cell has a rigid cellulose cell wall outside the membrane, whereas the cheek cell has only a thin membrane. The leaf cell has green chloroplasts and a large central vacuole, whereas the cheek cell has no chloroplasts and only small vacuoles.

questions.solution_md: Cell wall and chloroplasts or vacuole.

marking_scheme.step: Cell wall present in the leaf cell, absent in the cheek cell
Chloroplasts or large vacuole in the leaf cell only

questions.stem_md: State the cell theory in three points. Name the scientist who completed it and say what his addition was.

answer.model_answer_md: The cell theory says that all living things are made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life, and that all cells arise from cells that already exist. The last point was added by Rudolf Virchow in 1855. Schleiden and Schwann had earlier proposed that plants and animals are made of cells.

questions.solution_md: Three points; Virchow added that cells come from cells.

marking_scheme.step: Cell is the unit of structure and function

questions.stem_md: A photograph of a bacterial cell is taken at a magnification of 10000. The cell measures 20 mm in the photograph. Find the actual length of the bacterium in micrometres.
questions.solution_md: Actual size $= \dfrac{20\ \text{mm}}{10000} = 0.002\ \text{mm}$. Since $1\ \text{mm} = 1000\ \mu\text{m}$, this is $0.002\times 1000 = 2\ \mu\text{m}$, which lies in the usual 1 to 5 micrometre range for a bacterium.

marking_scheme.step: Divides the photograph size by the magnification

questions.stem_md: A microscope slide shows a cell that has a cell wall, ribosomes and DNA lying free in the cytoplasm, but no nuclear membrane and no mitochondria. The cell is most likely:

options.text_md: an onion root cell, which is eukaryotic
a human cheek cell, which is eukaryotic
a bacterial cell, which is prokaryotic
a yeast cell, which is eukaryotic

questions.solution_md: No nuclear membrane and no membrane-bound organelles mean a prokaryotic cell. Onion, human and yeast cells all have a true nucleus, so the answer is option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which pair contains only prokaryotes?

options.text_md: Yeast and Amoeba
A bacterium and a yeast
Spirogyra and Amoeba
Cyanobacteria and a soil bacterium

questions.solution_md: Cyanobacteria and soil bacteria have no true nucleus, so both are prokaryotes — option (d). Yeast, Amoeba and Spirogyra are all eukaryotes, which spoils the other pairs.

questions.stem_md: Under a microscope a student measures two unknown cells: cell M is about 2 µm long and cell N about 60 µm long, and both contain DNA. Which conclusion is best supported by the sizes alone?

options.text_md: Cell M is eukaryotic, because small cells always have a nucleus.
Cell M is more likely to be prokaryotic, because bacteria are usually 1 to 5 µm long.
Cell N is prokaryotic, because large cells have no nucleus.
Both are prokaryotic, because both contain DNA.

questions.solution_md: Prokaryotic cells are usually 1 to 5 µm and eukaryotic cells 10 to 100 µm, so size points to M as prokaryotic — option (b). Size is only a hint, and having DNA does not separate the two groups, since all cells contain DNA.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A bacterium and a human cell both contain DNA.

**Reason (R):** Both a bacterium and a human cell have a nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: All cells contain DNA, so A is true. A bacterium has no nuclear membrane, so R is false — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Where is the DNA found in a bacterium? Why is the bacterium called a prokaryote?

answer.model_answer_md: In a bacterium the DNA lies free in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid. It is called a prokaryote because it has no nuclear membrane around the DNA, so it has no true nucleus, and it also has no membrane-bound organelles.

questions.solution_md: Nucleoid; no true nucleus.

marking_scheme.step: DNA lies in the nucleoid in the cytoplasm
No nuclear membrane or true nucleus

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled sketch of a bacterial cell.

(b) Give three differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and one example of each kind of organism.

answer.model_answer_md: A bacterial cell sketch shows a cell wall, a cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, and a nucleoid of circular DNA with no nuclear membrane. A prokaryotic cell has no true nucleus, but a eukaryotic cell has a nucleus with a nuclear membrane. A prokaryotic cell has no membrane-bound organelles, but a eukaryotic cell has mitochondria, ER and a Golgi apparatus. Prokaryotic cells are small, about 1 to 5 micrometres, while eukaryotic cells are about 10 to 100 micrometres. Bacteria are prokaryotes; Amoeba, yeast, plants and animals are eukaryotes.

questions.solution_md: Labelled sketch, three differences and examples.

marking_scheme.step: Labelled sketch with at least four correct labels

questions.stem_md: A researcher colours only the organelle that releases energy from glucose in a living cell. Which organelle will be coloured?

options.text_md: Lysosome
Mitochondrion
Golgi apparatus
Nucleolus

questions.solution_md: Energy is released from glucose in respiration, which happens in the mitochondria — option (b). Lysosomes digest, the Golgi apparatus packs products and the nucleolus is inside the nucleus.

questions.stem_md: A white blood cell swallows a bacterium. Which organelle will break down the bacterium inside the cell?

options.text_md: Nucleus
Chloroplast
Lysosome
Rough endoplasmic reticulum

questions.solution_md: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down germs and worn-out parts — option (c). The nucleus controls the cell, chloroplasts are not found in animal cells, and the rough ER makes proteins.

questions.stem_md: The red colour of a ripe tomato is due to pigments held in which kind of plastid?

options.text_md: Chloroplast
Leucoplast
Lysosome
Chromoplast

questions.solution_md: Chromoplasts hold coloured pigments in ripe fruits and petals — option (d). Chloroplasts are green and leucoplasts are colourless.

questions.stem_md: A sperm cell swims by lashing its tail, and many mitochondria are packed near the base of the tail. The best reason is that the mitochondria:

options.text_md: digest food for the sperm
release the energy that the tail needs for movement
make proteins for the head
store water for the tail

questions.solution_md: Moving the tail needs a steady supply of energy, which mitochondria release from food — option (b). Digestion is done by lysosomes, protein making by ribosomes and storage by vacuoles.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the plant cell wall is correct?

options.text_md: It is made of cellulose and lets water and dissolved substances pass through freely.
It is made of lipids and decides which substances enter the cell.
It lies inside the cell membrane and surrounds the nucleus.
It is found in animal cells but not in plant cells.

questions.solution_md: The wall is made of cellulose and is fully permeable, so it protects and shapes the cell but does not select substances — option (a). Selecting is the job of the membrane, which lies inside the wall.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Mitochondria are found only in animal cells.

**Reason (R):** Mitochondria release energy from food.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Plant cells also respire and contain mitochondria, so A is false. R is a true statement about mitochondria — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Every cell of a banyan tree, including those of its roots, contains chloroplasts.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Chloroplasts are found in the green parts exposed to light. Cells deep in the roots have leucoplasts or no plastids with chlorophyll.

questions.stem_md: Colourless plastids that store starch, oil or protein are called ______.
questions.solution_md: Leucoplasts are colourless storage plastids, found for example in a potato tuber.

questions.stem_md: Match each organelle (column I) with its job (column II).

options.text_md: Nucleus
Golgi apparatus
Lysosome
Large plant vacuole

match_right.text_md: Modifies and packs products into vesicles
Stores cell sap and keeps the cell firm
Controls the cell and holds the DNA

questions.solution_md: Nucleus controls the cell; the Golgi apparatus packs products; a lysosome digests; the large vacuole stores sap and keeps the cell firm.

questions.stem_md: A protein is made on the ribosomes of a cell and is sent out of the cell. Name the two organelles it passes through before it leaves, in order, and say what each does.

answer.model_answer_md: The protein is made by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, which also carries it inside the cell. It then goes to the Golgi apparatus, which modifies and packs it into vesicles that carry it to the cell membrane and out of the cell.

questions.solution_md: Rough ER then Golgi apparatus, then vesicle.

marking_scheme.step: Rough ER makes and carries the protein
Golgi apparatus modifies and packs it in vesicles

questions.stem_md: Name the three kinds of plastid. For each, give one place in a plant where it is found and its job.

answer.model_answer_md: Chloroplasts are found in green leaves and carry out photosynthesis because they hold chlorophyll. Chromoplasts are found in petals and ripe fruits and give them their colours. Leucoplasts are colourless and found in storage organs such as potato tubers, where they store starch, oil or protein.

questions.solution_md: Three plastids with place and job.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a neat labelled diagram of a plant cell.

(b) Name any four organelles and state one function of each.

answer.model_answer_md: A labelled plant cell shows the cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, large central vacuole, chloroplasts, mitochondria, ER and Golgi apparatus. The nucleus holds the DNA and controls the cell. Mitochondria release energy from food in respiration. Chloroplasts hold chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis. The large vacuole stores cell sap and keeps the cell firm. The cell wall of cellulose gives shape and protection.

questions.solution_md: Labelled diagram, four organelles with functions.

marking_scheme.step: Neat diagram with at least six correct labels
A correct function for each of the four

questions.stem_md: A student makes a model of an animal cell. Explain how the nucleus, mitochondria, rough ER, Golgi apparatus and lysosomes work together when the cell makes and uses a protein, and name one part the model should NOT have that a plant cell model would.

answer.model_answer_md: The nucleus holds the DNA instructions. Ribosomes on the rough ER build the protein from these instructions. The Golgi apparatus modifies and packs it into vesicles. Mitochondria release the energy that all these steps need. Lysosomes digest worn-out parts, including damaged organelles, so the cell stays healthy. An animal cell model should not have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts or a large central vacuole, which belong in the plant cell model.

questions.solution_md: A link of the five organelles, then one plant-only part.

marking_scheme.step: Nucleus gives instructions and rough ER makes the protein
Mitochondria supply energy and lysosomes digest waste
One plant-only part, for example cell wall

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A student prepares three slides and records what she sees.

| Slide | Material | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| P | Thin peel from an onion bulb | Rectangular cells with thick walls, one large vacuole, no green bodies |
| Q | Leaf of the water plant *Hydrilla* | Green oval bodies seen moving along the cell edges |
| R | Scraping from the inside of her cheek | Rounded cells, thin boundary only, no green bodies |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) chloroplasts

**(b)** Slide R, because the cells have only a thin boundary and no cell wall or green bodies.

**(c)** (i) The onion bulb grows in the soil where there is no light, so its cells do not make chlorophyll and have no chloroplasts. Its cells have colourless plastids, leucoplasts, that store food such as starch, so no green bodies appear.

**OR** (ii) Cells of slide P have a thick cell wall and one large central vacuole. Cells of slide R have no cell wall, and their vacuoles are small or absent.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Green oval bodies in a leaf cell are chloroplasts, which hold the green pigment chlorophyll — option (c).

**(b)** R: no wall, no chloroplasts.

**(c)** (i) No light underground, so no chloroplasts; storage plastids instead.

(ii) Cell wall and large vacuole in P.

children.stem_md: The green oval bodies seen in slide Q are:

options.text_md: mitochondria
lysosomes
chloroplasts
nuclei

children.solution_md: Green oval bodies in a leaf cell are chloroplasts, which hold the green pigment chlorophyll — option (c).

children.stem_md: Which slide shows an animal cell? Give one reason from the table.

answer.model_answer_md: Slide R, because the cells have only a thin boundary and no cell wall or green bodies.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): The onion bulb grows underground, yet it is a plant. Explain why slide P shows no green bodies.

answer.model_answer_md: The onion bulb grows in the soil where there is no light, so its cells do not make chlorophyll and have no chloroplasts. Its cells have colourless plastids, leucoplasts, that store food such as starch, so no green bodies appear.

children.solution_md: No light underground, so no chloroplasts; storage plastids instead.

marking_scheme.step: Underground, no light, so no chloroplasts

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Give two features that would let you tell the cells of slide P from those of slide R.

answer.model_answer_md: Cells of slide P have a thick cell wall and one large central vacuole. Cells of slide R have no cell wall, and their vacuoles are small or absent.

alternatives.solution_md: Cell wall and large vacuole in P.

marking_scheme.step: Cell wall in P, absent in R
Large vacuole in P, small or none in R

questions.stem_md: Two beakers hold sugar solutions of 2 percent and 10 percent, separated by a membrane that only water can cross. In which direction is the net movement of water?

options.text_md: From the 2 percent solution to the 10 percent solution
From the 10 percent solution to the 2 percent solution
Sugar moves across and water does not
There is no movement of any kind

questions.solution_md: Water moves by osmosis towards the stronger solution, so it moves from the 2 percent side to the 10 percent side — option (a). Sugar cannot cross, and molecules keep moving, so (d) is wrong.

questions.stem_md: A student puts a piece of onion peel in a strong salt solution and sees the contents of each cell pulling away from the cell wall. This is called:

options.text_md: endosmosis
diffusion of the wall
plasmolysis
turgor

questions.solution_md: In a stronger solution the cell loses water by exosmosis and the protoplast shrinks away from the wall; this is plasmolysis — option (c). Endosmosis would swell the cell and turgor is firmness from water.

questions.stem_md: After heavy dosing with a very strong chemical fertiliser, the plants in a field wilt even though the soil is wet. The most likely reason is that:

options.text_md: the soil solution is weaker than the root cell sap, so water leaves the root cells
the soil solution is stronger than the root cell sap, so water leaves the root cells
the roots take in too much water and the cells burst
diffusion of fertiliser into the cells fills the vacuole

questions.solution_md: A very strong soil solution is hypertonic to the root cells, so water leaves them by exosmosis and the plant wilts — option (b). The reverse would make cells gain water.

questions.stem_md: A potato osmometer is set up with sugar in the cavity and the potato stands in water. After three hours the liquid level in the cavity has risen. What does this show?

options.text_md: Sugar has moved out of the cavity into the beaker.
The potato has made new water.
Water has entered the cavity from the beaker by osmosis.
Water has left the cavity and evaporated.

questions.solution_md: The sugar solution is stronger than the water outside, so water enters through the potato cells by osmosis and raises the level — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Dry raisins swell when they are soaked in water.

**Reason (R):** Diffusion does not need the cell to supply energy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: water enters raisins by osmosis. R is also true, but it does not explain why raisins swell — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When oxygen enters a cell by diffusion, the cell has to supply energy for the movement.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Diffusion is the movement of particles from higher to lower concentration, and it needs no energy from the cell.

questions.stem_md: A plant cell that has lost water so that its protoplast has shrunk away from the cell wall is said to be ______.
questions.solution_md: Loss of water in a hypertonic solution shrinks the protoplast away from the wall: the cell is plasmolysed.

questions.stem_md: A piece of radish with a mass of 8.0 g is kept in a 5 percent salt solution for one hour. Its mass is then 7.4 g. Find the percentage loss in mass.
questions.solution_md: Loss in mass $= 8.0 - 7.4 = 0.6\ \text{g}$. Percentage loss $= \dfrac{0.6}{8.0} \times 100 = 7.5$ percent. The loss shows that water left the cells by exosmosis.

marking_scheme.step: Finds the loss in mass, 0.6 g
Divides by the starting mass and multiplies by 100: 7.5

questions.stem_md: Two shell-less eggs of equal mass are placed one in pure water and one in a strong salt solution for an hour. State what happens to the mass of each egg and name the process.

answer.model_answer_md: The egg in pure water gains mass because water enters it by endosmosis. The egg in strong salt solution loses mass because water leaves it by exosmosis. In both cases water moves through the selectively permeable egg membrane by osmosis.

questions.solution_md: Gain in water, loss in salt solution.

marking_scheme.step: Egg in water swells and gains mass: endosmosis
Egg in salt solution shrinks and loses mass: exosmosis

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between diffusion and osmosis.

answer.model_answer_md: Diffusion can happen for any particles, such as gases or dissolved substances, and needs no membrane. Osmosis is the movement of water only, and it must take place through a selectively permeable membrane towards the stronger solution.

questions.solution_md: Which particles move, and the need for a membrane.

marking_scheme.step: Diffusion: any particles; osmosis: water only
Osmosis needs a selectively permeable membrane; diffusion does not

questions.stem_md: Describe a simple activity with dry raisins to show osmosis. State what you do, what you observe and what you conclude.

answer.model_answer_md: Weigh some dry raisins and divide them into two bowls, one with plain water and one with strong sugar solution. Leave them overnight, then weigh again. The raisins in plain water swell and gain mass, whereas those in the strong sugar solution stay shrunken. This shows that water moves through the raisin skin by osmosis towards the stronger solution.

questions.solution_md: Set-up, observation and conclusion.

marking_scheme.step: Raisins in plain water and in strong sugar solution
Raisins in water swell; others stay shrunken
Water moves by osmosis towards the stronger solution

questions.stem_md: A plant cell and an animal cell with no wall are placed in pure water. Explain why the plant cell becomes firm but stays whole, while the animal cell may swell and burst.

answer.model_answer_md: In pure water both cells take in water by endosmosis. In the plant cell the swelling protoplast presses against the rigid cellulose cell wall, which resists and stops it bursting, so the cell becomes turgid and firm. questions.stem_md: Describe how you would show osmosis using a potato osmometer. Draw a labelled diagram and write the apparatus, the procedure, the observation and the conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md: Take a large potato, peel it and scoop out a cavity. Put some sugar solution in the cavity and mark its level with a pin. Stand the potato in a beaker of water. After a few hours the level in the cavity has risen above the pin. A labelled diagram shows the potato, the cavity with sugar solution, the pin marking the level and the water in the beaker. The conclusion is that water entered the cavity through the potato cells by osmosis, towards the stronger sugar solution.

questions.solution_md: Diagram, procedure, observation and conclusion.

questions.stem_md: A cell can be kept in a weaker solution, an equal solution or a stronger solution. For each case, state the term for the solution, what happens to the water movement and what a plant cell looks like. Name the processes involved.

answer.model_answer_md: In a weaker, hypotonic solution water enters the cell by endosmosis, and a plant cell swells and becomes turgid. In an equal, isotonic solution there is no net movement of water, and the cell stays firm but not swollen. In a stronger, hypertonic solution water leaves the cell by exosmosis. A plant cell then shrinks and its protoplast pulls away from the wall, which is called plasmolysis.

questions.solution_md: Three solutions with term, movement and appearance.

marking_scheme.step: Isotonic: no net movement, firm cell

| Salt in solution (percent) | Mass at start (g) | Mass after one hour (g) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 8.0 | 8.8 |
| 2 | 8.0 | 8.2 |
| 4 | 8.0 | 7.6 |
| 6 | 8.0 | 7.2 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) a hypotonic solution, so it gained water

**(b)** Change is 7.6 minus 8.0, which is −0.4 g, so the percentage change is −0.4 divided by 8.0 times 100, that is -5.0 percent (a loss of 5.0 percent).

**(c)** (i) Between 2 and 4 percent the change goes from +2.5 to -5.0 percent, a swing of 7.5 over 2 units. Zero is reached 2.5 ÷ 7.5 of the way, so the strength is about 2.7 percent.

**(b)** (7.6 − 8.0) ÷ 8.0 × 100 = -5.0 percent.

**(c)** (i) 2 + 2 × (2.5 ÷ 7.5) ≈ 2.7 percent.

(ii) Plain water makes the carrot gain water; salt beyond 2.7 percent makes it lose.

4 and 4

questions.solution_md: The adult grows by mitosis, so its body cells keep 8 chromosomes. A sperm is made by meiosis and has half, 4 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A clinic advertises that stem cell treatment can cure every disease. Which response is best supported at present?

options.text_md: The claim is correct, because stem cells can become any cell and so can cure everything.
Stem cells cannot divide, so they have no medical use at all.
Stem cells are used in some treatments, such as bone marrow transplants for blood diseases, but many other claims are still under research.
Stem cells exist only in embryos and cannot be used in adults.

questions.solution_md: Bone marrow transplant is an established use, while many other uses are being researched, so an all-disease cure is not supported — option (c). Stem cells can divide, and adults also have them.

questions.stem_md: Why can an electron microscope show organelles in much finer detail than a school light microscope?

options.text_md: It uses glowing dyes to colour living cells.
It uses a beam of electrons and can show much smaller details.
It uses sunlight with stronger mirrors.
It makes cells divide so that they look bigger.

questions.solution_md: An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons and resolves details far too small for light — option (b). Glowing dyes belong to fluorescence microscopy, and microscopes do not make cells divide.

questions.solution_md: Worn-out cells are replaced by new ones made by mitosis, so R correctly explains A — option (a).

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

False

questions.stem_md: The stage of mitosis in which the chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell is called ______.
questions.solution_md: Chromosomes line up at the equator in metaphase, are pulled apart in anaphase.

questions.stem_md: A pea root-tip cell has 14 chromosomes and divides by mitosis 3 times in a row. What is the total number of chromosomes in all the cells formed?
questions.solution_md: Each mitosis doubles the number of cells, so 3 rounds give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cells. Each cell keeps 14 chromosomes, so the total is 8 × 14 = 112.

answer.model_answer_md: The division is mitosis. Cells near the wound divide by mitosis to make many new cells that are identical to the old ones, with the same number of chromosomes. These new cells replace the damaged ones and close the cut, so the skin is repaired.

questions.stem_md: Suppose gametes were made by mitosis instead of meiosis. What would happen to the chromosome number of the zygote in each generation? How does meiosis prevent this problem?

answer.model_answer_md: If gametes were made by mitosis, each would have the full number. Two gametes would then give a zygote with double the number, and the number would keep doubling in every generation. Meiosis prevents this because it halves the chromosome number in each gamete, so fertilisation brings it back to the normal number.

questions.solution_md: Doubling each generation unless meiosis halves the number.

questions.stem_md: Compare mitosis and meiosis on five points. A cell of a certain plant has 12 chromosomes; state how many cells and how many chromosomes in each cell result from one mitosis and from one meiosis.

answer.model_answer_md: Mitosis takes place in body cells, but meiosis takes place in reproductive organs. Mitosis has one division and meiosis has two. Mitosis gives two cells and meiosis gives four. Mitosis keeps the chromosome number and meiosis halves it. Mitosis serves growth and repair, and meiosis makes gametes. For a cell with 12 chromosomes, mitosis gives 2 cells with 12 each, and meiosis gives 4 cells with 6 each.

questions.solution_md: Five points; 2 cells of 12 and 4 cells of 6.

marking_scheme.step: Five correct points of comparison, one-half mark each
